what: VSE Corporation distributes aircraft parts and repairs aviation components. It supplies parts to airlines and maintenance shops, holds distribution rights from engine and component makers, and performs repair and overhaul work on aircraft parts in its own facilities.
customers: Commercial airlines, business aviation operators, maintenance and repair organisations, and the original equipment makers whose parts it distributes under licence.
money: Aircraft parts distribution under licence from component manufacturers.
Repair and overhaul of aircraft components in its own shops.
moat: Exclusive distribution agreements from engine and component makers are the asset: the manufacturer appoints one distributor for a part line, and that appointment is both hard to win and hard to lose. Repair capability for a specific component also requires regulatory approval for that part, which is a slow, expensive qualification a competitor must repeat.
risks: Free cash flow of only $27.5M against $118.4M of net income, and 184.6 times free cash flow — the company is consuming cash building parts inventory.
The shares trade at about 44.3 times earnings and 22.5 times EV/EBITDA, which is a very full price.
Last year’s net margin was 1.1%, reflecting the transition and acquisition costs of reshaping the business toward aviation.
Revenue history is erratic — $669.4M in 2022, $544.0M in 2023, $1.1B in 2025 — because segments have been bought and sold.
Nine analysts average a $247.78 target against a $180.61 price, a 37% gap.
opportunities: Revenue has grown strongly in aviation, reaching $1.1B in 2025 with trailing revenue of $1.6B.
Exclusive distribution agreements are durable positions that manufacturers rarely reassign.
Repair approvals for specific components are regulatory qualifications a competitor must earn separately.
Debt of $342.8M against $69.4M of cash is manageable relative to the cash generation potential.
Aircraft fleets are older than they have ever been, and older aircraft need more parts and more repair work.
watch: Aviation revenue growth and the conversion of earnings into cash. The inventory build is the current drag, and whether it converts determines the real return.
view: VSE has spent several years turning itself from a mixed government services and distribution company into an aviation parts and repair business, and the financial history reflects the surgery rather than the result: revenue of $669 million, then $544 million, then $1.1 billion, as segments were sold and acquired. Anyone reading the trend is reading corporate restructuring, not operating performance.

The aviation aftermarket is a genuinely good place to be. Exclusive distribution agreements are the central asset: a component manufacturer appoints one distributor for a part line, which is hard to win and, once established, hard to lose. Repair capability is similarly protected, because performing an overhaul on a specific part requires a regulatory approval that a competitor must obtain separately and slowly. And the structural tailwind is real — the global aircraft fleet is older than it has ever been, because new aircraft deliveries have run behind demand for years, and old aircraft consume more parts and more repair hours.

The number that stops me is the cash conversion: $27 million of free cash flow against $118 million of net income, which is 185 times free cash flow. The explanation is almost certainly inventory — a parts distributor must buy and hold stock before it can sell it, and a growing distributor consumes cash doing so. That is a legitimate use of capital and it is not a loss. But it means the reported earnings are not yet cash, and at 44.3 times earnings the price assumes they will be.

So this is a good business in a good part of the cycle at a price that leaves nothing for disappointment. Nine analysts at $247.78 against $180.61 are modelling the aviation growth continuing. What I would want before paying this multiple is a year or two of earnings converting into cash, which would confirm the inventory build was growth rather than drag.
bull: An ageing global fleet drives parts and repair demand into exclusive distribution rights, and the inventory build converts to cash as growth matures.
bear: The inventory build keeps consuming cash, a distribution agreement is lost, and a 44 times earnings multiple on 1% margins has far to fall.
